slides.title: Understanding Wren Phonics
bullets: How we teach your child to read and spell
What you’ll see come home, and why
How you can help — no training needed
slides.notes: Welcome families warmly. Say how long the session will run (aim for 30-40 minutes including questions) and that there will be time for questions throughout, not just at the end.

slides.title: Why we’re here tonight
bullets: Phonics is how your child is taught to read at school
You will see it in every book, letter and record we send home
Understanding it means you can support it with confidence
slides.notes: Keep this brief — one slide of context before getting into the actual content. Reassure: nobody needs a teaching background to follow tonight.

slides.title: What is phonics?
bullets: Spoken words are made of small sounds (phonemes)
Letters/letter-groups spell those sounds (graphemes)
Reading = blending sounds together, left to right
Spelling = the same thing in reverse
slides.notes: Demo live: say "c-a-t" slowly as three separate sounds, then blend them into "cat". Ask the room to try it with you on a second word, e.g. "s-u-n".

slides.title: Our approach
bullets: One programme for Reception and Year 1, with an outline for Year 2
One sequence, one daily routine, one set of books
Written to the DfE’s 16 core criteria for phonics programmes
slides.notes: If asked about validation: Wren Phonics is written to the DfE’s 16 core criteria, but it is not a DfE-validated programme — the DfE has closed validation rounds.

slides.title: Phase 1–6, in plain English
bullets: Phase 1 — "Introduction": listening and sound-play, no letters yet
Phases 2–4 — "Learning": the alphabetic code, taught directly
Phases 5–6 — "School Readiness": extra spellings, suffixes, prefixes
slides.notes: Families may already know the "Phase 1-6" labels from elsewhere — lead with those, then introduce Wren's plain-English names for the three stages they group into. Reassure it's the same underlying sequence either way.

slides.title: It starts before letters
bullets: Listening walks, rhymes, body-percussion games
Tuning children’s ears in to sounds around them
No letters at all — and that’s exactly right at this stage
slides.notes: If any nursery-age families are present, this is their slide — reassure that Ofsted does not expect phonics teaching in nursery, and this listening work is the genuine groundwork for it.

slides.title: Pure sounds
bullets: "Bouncy" sounds: quick and clipped (t, p, b...)
"Stretchy" sounds: held as long as you like (s, f, m...)
Never add an extra "uh" on the end
slides.notes: Demo both: say "t" cleanly, then say "tuh" and ask the room to notice how it changes blending ("c-a-tuh" doesn’t become "cat" as cleanly as "c-a-t" does). Point to the family pronunciation-guide handout for every sound.

slides.title: Blending: reading
bullets: Say each sound once, left to right
Then run it together at normal speed
Never a chant with no blend at the end
slides.notes: Demo on a whiteboard/flipchart word if you have one taught sound set in common with the room’s children’s stage, e.g. "sat" for an early Reception audience.

slides.title: Segmenting: spelling
bullets: Say the whole word once first
Then say it sound by sound, writing as you go
Exactly blending, in reverse
slides.notes: If time allows, invite one volunteer to "spell" a simple word aloud sound by sound before you write it, to make the mirror with blending concrete.

slides.title: Sound buttons
bullets: A dot under a single-letter sound
A bar under a two/three-letter team
Helps a child see where one sound ends and the next begins
slides.notes: Show a printed example from a reading-practice book if you have one — point out a dot (e.g. under "s") next to a bar (e.g. under "sh").

slides.title: Tricky words
bullets: Some words can’t yet be fully sounded out (e.g. "the")
We read the word, name the tricky part, then spell it
Never sounded out from scratch
slides.notes: Give one concrete example: "the" — the "e" doesn’t say its usual sound. Reassure this is a SMALL, carefully scheduled list, not a free-for-all of whole-word memorising.

slides.title: A typical lesson
bullets: Warm up — quick revisit of recent sounds
New sound — taught directly, with a mnemonic and action
Have a go — read and spell words with it
Use it — a sentence to read, a sentence to write
slides.notes: Same four-part shape every single day, so children always know what’s coming — that predictability is doing real work for anxious or EAL learners especially.

slides.title: Why the first book looks so simple
bullets: Only uses sounds already taught — nothing ahead
A tiny book is correct, not a concern
Books grow as the taught code grows
slides.notes: This is one of the most common parent worries — spend real time here. Show an example of an early book next to a later one if you have copies.

slides.title: Reading practice at school: 3 sessions
bullets: Sound it out — the first, careful read
Read it with feeling — reading with expression
Talk about it — what it meant
slides.notes: Emphasise: SAME book, three times — that repetition is deliberate, not a sign the child is behind.

slides.title: The two books at home
bullets: Reading practice book: your child reads to YOU
Sharing book: YOU read to your child, for fun
Both matter — for different reasons
slides.notes: Point to the separate "two kinds of book" letter going home — this slide is a preview, not the full explanation.

slides.title: How you can help
bullets: Give time to sound out before helping
Prompt "what’s the first sound?", don’t supply the word
Praise effort, not just getting it right first try
Little and often beats one long session
slides.notes: Keep this practical and short — these are the exact tips on the reading-record booklet, so families will see them again at home.

slides.title: Checking progress
bullets: Half-termly reviews of everything taught so far
Individual records — never just a whole-group tick list
"Same-day boost" catches a gap the day it appears
slides.notes: If asked how they’ll know how their own child is doing: point to the half-termly reports/parents’ evening conversations, not just this workshop.

slides.title: The Phonics Screening Check
bullets: A short, untimed check in June of Year 1
40 words, one-to-one, with someone your child knows
No fixed "pass mark" — it’s set freshly each year
slides.notes: This is the anxiety slide — go slowly, invite questions here specifically. See the separate PSC handout for full detail; do not quote a specific past year’s mark as if it still applies.

slides.title: SEND and EAL
bullets: Same programme for every child
We adapt the DELIVERY — pace, repetition, support
Never a different programme or a skipped sequence
slides.notes: If a parent raises a specific need, offer a 1:1 follow-up conversation rather than trying to resolve it in the room.

slides.title: Questions
bullets: What would you like to know more about?
Handouts tonight: phonics explained, pronunciation guide, the two-books letter, the PSC guide
slides.notes: Leave real time for this — at least 10 minutes. If a question needs a longer answer, offer to follow up individually rather than letting the room run long.

slides.title: Thank you
bullets: Thank you for coming, and for reading with your child
Your child’s teacher is always happy to talk
More resources: getwren.co.uk
slides.notes: End warmly and on time. Hand out the printed family resources as people leave if you haven’t already.
